title: Work, Careers and Applying
overview: Write the part of an application that actually gets read. Say what you did rather than what you are like, and put a number on the result. Answer a question that wants evidence with a four-part case, and ask questions of your own at the end. Then describe where you worked and who you wrote to, in one sentence.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account by somebody who reads applications, a writing guide and a completed application.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Describe the place you worked or the person you wrote to
Answer an interview question with a real example
Ask an employer something useful at the end
Tell whether a CV phrase says anything checkable
Say how much better a result was, and than what
Write an application that says what you did
Say technician and electrician so they are understood
lectureScript:
This unit closes Stage 8, and it is the most directly useful one in the level.
It is about applying for work, and about the small number of things that decide whether anybody reads what you wrote.

The reading opens with somebody who reads four hundred applications a year and has stopped pretending they read them all properly.
What they read properly is the top third of the first page.
So the profile is the most valuable space on the document, and most people fill it with nothing at all.
Self-motivated. Hard-working. Detail-oriented. Results-driven.
There is a test in that reading worth carrying out of this unit, and it is one question.
Would anybody write the opposite?
Nobody has ever sent a CV saying they are poorly organised and easily distracted.
So those words carry no information, and they are occupying the one part of the page that decides whether you are read at all.

That is the fourth card. Unit 2 taught you to build a hyphenated adjective, and a CV is full of them.
They split into two kinds, sharply.
The ones that describe YOU prove nothing, because everybody claims them.
The ones that describe the WORK carry information, because not everybody can claim them.
A three-year secondment. A client-facing role. A fully qualified electrician. A cross-site rollout.
Each of those is a fact somebody could ask you about, which is the whole point.

The fifth card follows directly. Unit 2 also taught you to put a degree word on a comparison: much cheaper, far better.
That says the gap is big. It does not say how big, and a number is what gets remembered.
Twice as many enquiries as last year. Twelve per cent above target. Half the downtime we had before.
By far the most reliable of the three. One of the most experienced technicians on site.
That last one has a trap: one of the most always takes a plural noun, because you are picking one out of a group.
And there is a warning on all of these. Every comparison invites the question compared with what.
We had twice as many enquiries is not a claim. It is half of one.

The second card is about the question an interview actually asks.
Unit 4 gave you the follow-up question and the polite indirect question. This is a third kind.
Tell me about a time when you had to work to a deadline.
That is not asking whether you are good at deadlines. Everybody says yes to that.
It wants one real occasion, and there is a shape that answers it. Four sentences.
The situation. What you were asked to do. What you did. The result, with a number in it.
Watch the third one, because it is where most answers fail. It has to say what YOU did, not what the team did.
And there is a second kind of question that looks similar and is not.
What would you do if a delivery arrived late? That has not happened. It is a scenario, and you answer it with a second conditional, from the unit before this one.

The third card is the question at the end, which almost every candidate wastes.
Do you have any questions for us? Most people say no, and it is scored, and it reads as a lack of interest even when it is politeness.
Have three ready. Ask two. Keep the third in case one gets answered.
Ask about the work itself, or about the problem they are trying to solve, or about what happens next.
And there is one question worth more than any other.
Is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?
That lets you repair a doubt before it becomes a decision. If they have one, they will say it. If not, you have lost nothing.
Pay and holiday are real questions and they belong to the offer, not to the interview.

The first card is the grammar you need for all of this, and it is the last piece of relative clauses.
You have built them four times and never with a preposition in one.
The company I worked for. The person I sent it to. That is the everyday version, and it is correct.
You may have been told never to end a sentence with a preposition. That rule was invented in the seventeenth century by somebody who admired Latin, and it has never described English.
There is a formal version, and you need to be able to read it.
The company for which I worked. The person to whom it was sent.
One thing changes when the preposition moves to the front. Who becomes whom, and it is not optional.
The person to who it was sent is wrong. In a contract, expect the formal one. In an email, use the short one.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 practice, four or more of six; Practice 2 four or more of five; Speaking 3 recording; Writing 2; Quiz items 3, 4 and 12.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can answer an interview question with a real example rather than a claim.

outcomes.evidence: Pattern 3 practice, four or more of six; Practice 3 five or more of seven; Speaking 5 recording; Quiz item 5.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can ask an employer something useful at the end of an interview.

outcomes.outcome: Tell a compound adjective that carries information from one that anybody could claim.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 4 practice, eight or more of ten; Practice 4 ten or more of twelve; Writing 3; comprehension questions 1 to 3; Quiz items 6 and 7.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can tell whether a phrase on a CV says anything a reader could check.

outcomes.outcome: Stress a job name built with -ician, -ist or -ant where a listener expects it.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 2 recording; Speaking 6 two-minute turn; self-assessment.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say technician and electrician so they are understood first time.

words.meaning: A person trained to work with technical equipment.
words.example: Two technicians cover the whole site.
practice: -ician names a person by a skill: technician, electrician, musician.
The stress falls just before the ending: tech-NI-cian.
A technician maintains; an engineer designs.
Its adjective is technical.
words.tutor: Describe what a technician does. Ask the tutor where the stress fell.

words.meaning: A person who installs and repairs electrical systems.
words.example: You will need a qualified electrician for that.
practice: -ician again, and the stress moves the same way.
Electrician comes from electric, dropping the c sound.
It is a protected trade in many places.
An electrical engineer is a different job.
words.starter: You will need an electrician to …
words.tutor: Say what needs an electrician. Ask the tutor about the stress.

words.meaning: An expert brought in to advise, usually from outside.
words.example: They brought in a consultant for six weeks.
practice: -ant and -ent name a person by what they do.
A consultant advises; they usually do not implement.
Its verb is consult, which takes a direct object.
In medicine, a consultant is a senior doctor.
words.starter: They brought in a consultant to …
words.tutor: Say why a consultant was brought in. Ask the tutor what they would not do.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to examine information in detail.
words.example: The analyst found the pattern in the returns.
practice: -ist names a person by a field: analyst, specialist, scientist.
Its verb is analyse, with an s in British English.
Its noun for the work is analysis, plural analyses.
An analyst examines; a technician fixes.
words.tutor: Say what an analyst found. Ask the tutor to check the spelling of analyse.

words.meaning: A person who concentrates on one narrow area.
words.example: We need a specialist for the older machines.
practice: Specialist takes in for the field: a specialist in seals.
It is also an adjective: specialist equipment.
Its verb is specialise, which takes in.
A specialist knows one thing deeply.
words.tutor: Say what kind of specialist is needed. Ask the tutor to check the preposition.

words.meaning: A person who practises a profession or a skill.
words.example: She is a practitioner of the old method.
practice: Practitioner comes from practise, the verb with an s.
The noun practice has a c; the verb practise has an s.
A practitioner does the work rather than teaching it.
It is formal: general practitioner is the commonest use.
words.tutor: Describe a practitioner. Ask the tutor about practice and practise.

words.meaning: A short summary of who you are, at the top of a CV.
words.example: Keep the profile to three lines.
practice: A profile is the opening paragraph of a CV.
It should say what you do, not what you are like.
It is also a verb: to profile somebody.
A raised profile means more people know about you.
words.tutor: Write a profile line. Ask the tutor whether it said what you DO.

words.meaning: A person who will confirm what you say about yourself.
words.example: Both referees were contacted the same week.
practice: A referee vouches for you; a reference is what they write.
In sport a referee is something else entirely.
Always ask a referee before naming them.
Its plural is referees.
words.tutor: Name your referees. Ask the tutor about referee and reference.

words.meaning: A collection of work you show to prove what you can do.
words.example: The portfolio matters more than the profile here.
practice: A portfolio shows work; a CV describes it.
It is used in design, building, teaching and writing.
Its plural is portfolios.
A portfolio of responsibilities is a separate sense.
words.tutor: Describe a portfolio. Ask the tutor how it differs from a CV.

words.meaning: A qualification or document proving what you can do.
words.example: Bring your credentials to the first meeting.
practice: Credentials is usually plural.
A credential is proof, not a claim.
It comes from the same root as credible.
Digital credentials are increasingly common.
words.tutor: List some credentials. Ask the tutor whether they were proof or claims.

words.meaning: A period of supervised work as part of training.
words.example: The placement lasted eight weeks.
practice: A placement is training; a job is not.
It comes from place, with -ment.
You do a placement, or you are on placement.
Placements are often unpaid, which is worth knowing.
words.tutor: Describe a placement. Ask the tutor how it differs from a job.

words.meaning: A temporary move to another job or department.
words.example: She is on secondment to the northern site.
practice: On secondment is the fixed phrase.
Its verb is second, stressed differently: se-COND.
A secondment ends and you go back.
It is British: other countries use different words.
words.tutor: Describe a secondment. Ask the tutor where the stress falls on the verb.

words.meaning: To organise several people or parts so they work together.
words.example: I coordinated the move across three sites.
practice: Coordinate takes a direct object.
Its noun is coordination.
Coordinating is organising others; doing is not.
It is one of the most useful CV verbs.
words.tutor: Say what you coordinated. Ask the tutor whether it involved other people.

words.meaning: To be responsible for watching that work is done properly.
words.example: I oversaw two teams for a year.
practice: Its past forms are oversaw and overseen.
Overseeing is supervising without doing it yourself.
Do not confuse it with overlook, which means to miss.
It is stronger than coordinate: it implies authority.
words.tutor: Say what you oversaw. Ask the tutor about oversee and overlook.

words.meaning: To make a process simpler and quicker.
words.example: We streamlined the checking process.
practice: Streamline takes a direct object.
It implies removing steps, not adding staff.
It is a single word.
Streamlining should be followed by a number.
words.tutor: Say what you streamlined. Ask the tutor whether you gave a number.

words.meaning: To put a plan or a decision into practice.
words.example: The new system was implemented in March.
practice: Implement takes a direct object.
Its noun is implementation.
Deciding is not implementing: the second is the hard part.
It is also a noun, meaning a tool, stressed differently.
words.tutor: Say what you implemented. Ask the tutor how it differs from deciding.

words.meaning: To discuss something in order to reach an agreement.
words.example: I negotiated the contract with two suppliers.
practice: Negotiate takes a direct object, and with for the other party.
Its noun is negotiation.
Negotiating implies both sides moved.
It also means to get past an obstacle.
words.tutor: Say what you negotiated and with whom. Ask the tutor whether both sides moved.

words.meaning: To keep in contact with another group to work together.
words.example: I liaised between the yard and the office.
practice: Liaise takes with a person, and between two groups.
Its noun is liaison.
Watch the spelling: two i's, liaise.
Liaising is communicating, not deciding.
words.tutor: Say who you liaised with. Ask the tutor to check the spelling.

words.meaning: To go beyond a limit or a target.
words.example: We exceeded the target by twelve per cent.
practice: Exceed takes a direct object, and by for the amount.
Exceeding a target is good; exceeding a limit is not.
Its adjective is excessive, which is always negative.
Always follow exceed with a number.
words.tutor: State something you exceeded. Ask the tutor whether you gave a number.

words.meaning: To do better than something or somebody else.
words.example: The second quarter surpassed the first.
practice: Surpass compares two things; exceed compares to a target.
It takes a direct object.
It is formal and slightly literary.
Unsurpassed means better than all others.
words.tutor: Say what surpassed what. Ask the tutor about surpass and exceed.

words.meaning: To keep something going at the same level.
words.example: We sustained that rate for eight months.
practice: Sustain takes a direct object, and often a period.
Its adjective is sustainable.
Sustaining is harder than achieving, and worth saying.
It also means to suffer: sustained an injury.
words.tutor: State something you sustained. Ask the tutor whether you gave a period.

words.meaning: To keep something or somebody you might have lost.
words.example: We retained all four clients that year.
practice: Retain takes a direct object.
Its noun is retention.
Retaining staff is the opposite of turnover.
It is formal: keep is the everyday word.
words.tutor: State something you retained. Ask the tutor what it would have cost to lose it.

words.meaning: To produce something, especially income or work.
words.example: The change generated eleven new enquiries.
practice: Generate takes a direct object.
Its noun is generation, which also means an age group.
It suits income, interest, work and electricity.
Always follow generate with a number.
words.tutor: State something you generated. Ask the tutor whether the number was there.

words.meaning: To reduce something as far as possible.
words.example: The change minimised downtime.
practice: Minimise takes a direct object.
It is spelled with an s in British English.
Minimising is reducing, not removing.
Its opposite is maximise.
words.tutor: State something you minimised. Ask the tutor whether it was reduced or removed.

words.meaning: A skill an employer has decided to test for.
words.example: The four competencies are listed on the form.
practice: A competency is a named, tested skill.
Its plural is competencies.
A competency question asks for an example, not an opinion.
Competence, without the y, means being good enough.
words.tutor: Name some competencies. Ask the tutor how a competency question works.

words.meaning: A situation described so you can say what you would do.
words.example: They gave me a scenario about a late delivery.
practice: A scenario is hypothetical: it has not happened.
It is answered with a second conditional, from Unit 13.
Its plural is scenarios.
A worst-case scenario is the fixed phrase.
words.starter: They gave me a scenario about …
words.tutor: Describe a scenario question. Ask the tutor which tense answers it.

words.meaning: An easy, comfortable relationship with somebody.
words.example: We built a rapport quite quickly.
practice: Rapport takes with.
The final t is silent: ra-POR.
You build or establish a rapport.
It is uncountable: not a rapports.
words.tutor: Describe building rapport. Ask the tutor how to pronounce it.

words.meaning: Able to express ideas clearly.
words.example: She was articulate under pressure.
practice: As an adjective it ends in -ate said quickly.
As a verb, to articulate, the ending is said fully.
Being articulate is about clarity, not vocabulary.
It is a common word in interview feedback.
words.tutor: Describe somebody articulate. Ask the tutor about the two pronunciations.

words.meaning: Saying what is needed in few words.
words.example: Keep the answer concise: two minutes at most.
practice: Concise is short AND complete.
Brief is only short; concise is short enough and no shorter.
Its noun is concision, or conciseness.
Concise answers are remembered; long ones are not.
words.tutor: Give a concise answer. Ask the tutor whether anything necessary was lost.

grammar.title: The company I worked for, or the company for which I worked
grammar.explanation:
You have built relative clauses four times in this course. None of them had
a PREPOSITION in it, and a great many real ones do.
There are two ways to write them. One is what everybody says. The other is
what contracts and formal letters use, and you need to be able to read it.
grammar.rule:
THE EVERYDAY WAY — the preposition goes at the END:
the company I worked for
the person I sent it to
the site we moved from
That is correct, standard, and what you should write in almost everything.

THE FORMAL WAY — the preposition goes in FRONT, and who becomes whom:
the company FOR WHICH I worked
the person TO WHOM it was sent
the site FROM WHICH we moved
Whom is compulsory here. for who is wrong in this pattern.

WHERE and WHEN replace in which and on which:
the site where we worked   = the site at which we worked
the day when it happened   = the day on which it happened

In the everyday version you can usually drop the relative word entirely:
the company (that) I worked for
In the formal version you can never drop anything.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these two ways: I worked for a company. It closed in 2019.
1. Everyday: keep the preposition at the end and drop the relative word.
   The company I worked for closed in 2019.
2. Formal: move for to the front. It now needs which after it.
   The company for which I worked closed in 2019.
Answer: both are correct. The first is what you would say. The second is
what you would meet in a contract.
grammar.mistake:
who cannot follow a preposition. It has to be whom.
No: the person to who it was sent.
Yes: the person to whom it was sent.
Or, everyday: the person it was sent to. That needs no whom at all.
grammar.tip: Preposition at the end for speech. Preposition in front, plus whom or which, for a contract.
grammar.practice:
Write each one twice: the everyday way and the formal way.
1. I worked for a company. It closed in 2019.
2. I sent it to a person. They never replied.
3. We moved from a site. It is now a car park.
4. She reported to a manager. He has since left.
Now rewrite these using where or when.
5. the site at which we worked
6. the day on which it happened
Now correct this.
7. the person to who it was sent
grammar.answers:
1. The company I worked for closed in 2019. / The company for which I worked closed in 2019.
2. The person I sent it to never replied. / The person to whom I sent it never replied.
3. The site we moved from is now a car park. / The site from which we moved is now a car park.
4. The manager she reported to has since left. / The manager to whom she reported has since left.
5. the site where we worked  6. the day when it happened
7. the person to whom it was sent.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Asking for a case, not an opinion
grammar.explanation:
Unit 4 taught the follow-up question and the polite indirect question.
An interview uses a third kind, and once you recognise it you can answer it
properly instead of guessing what is wanted.
It asks for a real event, not for an opinion about yourself.
grammar.rule:
THE COMPETENCY QUESTION — it wants one real example:
Tell me about a time when you had to work to a deadline.
Give me an example of a problem you solved.
Describe a situation where you disagreed with a decision.

What it is NOT asking:
Are you good at working to deadlines?  (an opinion, and everybody says yes)

THE SHAPE THAT ANSWERS IT — four parts, in order:
1. the situation, in one sentence
2. what YOU were asked to do
3. what YOU did, with a verb from group 3
4. the result, with a NUMBER

'We were two staff short over the August shutdown.
I was asked to cover the checking.
I streamlined the order of the checks and liaised with the yard directly.
We finished a day early and the backlog cleared by the 3rd.'

THE SCENARIO QUESTION is different: it has not happened.
What would you do if a delivery arrived late?
That one is answered with a second conditional, from Unit 13.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Answer this: tell me about a time when you had to work to a deadline.
1. Is it asking for an event or an opinion? An event.
2. So do not say I am good at deadlines. Pick one real occasion.
3. Situation, task, action, result. Four sentences.
4. Put a number in the result, because the result is what is remembered.
Answer: the four-sentence example above.
Notice that I appears in sentences two and three, and we in the result.
grammar.mistake:
The commonest failure is answering with a claim instead of a case.
Weak: I work well under pressure and I am very organised.
Better: We were two staff short in August, and I was asked to cover the checking.
Anybody can say the first. Only you can say the second.
grammar.tip: Situation, task, action, result. And a number in the result.
grammar.practice:
For each question, write the FOUR parts in note form. One line each.
1. Tell me about a time when you had to work to a deadline.
2. Give me an example of a problem you solved.
3. Describe a situation where you disagreed with a decision.
Now say which of these is a scenario question rather than a competency one.
4. What would you do if a delivery arrived late?
5. Tell me about a time when a delivery arrived late.
Now rewrite this weak answer as a case.
6. 'I work well under pressure and I am very organised.'
grammar.answers:
1 to 3: yours will differ. Each should have a situation, a task, an action
with a verb like coordinated, streamlined or liaised, and a result with a number.
4. A scenario question. It has not happened, so answer it with a second conditional.
5. A competency question. It has happened, so answer it with a real case.
6. Any four-part example will do. If your version has no number in it, add one.
4 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Do you have any questions for us?
grammar.explanation:
Almost every interview ends with this, and almost every candidate says no.
It is not a courtesy. It is the last question, and it is scored.
What you need is the shape of a question that can only be asked by somebody
who has thought about the job rather than about getting it.
grammar.rule:
THE THREE SHAPES THAT WORK

1. About the WORK itself:
   What does a typical week look like in this post?
   Which part of this job takes the most time?
   What would you want done in the first three months?

2. About the PROBLEM they are trying to solve:
   What made the post become available?
   What has made this difficult to fill?
   What would make you say, in a year, that this had gone well?

3. About what happens NEXT:
   When would you expect to decide?
   Is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?

That last one is the most useful question in the set, because it lets you
repair a doubt before it becomes a decision.

WHAT NOT TO ASK FIRST: pay, holiday, hours. Those are real and they belong
to the offer, not to the interview.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You sense they are unsure about your lack of experience with one system.
1. Can you raise it yourself? Not directly: that draws attention to it.
2. But you can invite them to raise it.
3. Use the shape that opens the door without naming the doubt.
Answer: Is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?
If the doubt is real, they will say it, and you get to answer it. If it is
not, you have lost nothing.
grammar.mistake:
No, I think you have covered everything is the answer that costs most.
It reads as a lack of interest even when it is politeness.
Have three questions ready. Ask two. Keep the third in case one is answered.
grammar.tip: Ask about the work, the problem, or what happens next. Have three ready.
grammar.practice:
Write one question of each kind for a job you invent.
1. About the work itself.
2. About the problem they are trying to solve.
3. About what happens next.
Now answer these.
4. Which single question lets you repair a doubt before it becomes a decision?
5. Why is 'no, you have covered everything' a poor answer?
6. Name two things that belong to the offer rather than the interview.
grammar.answers:
1 to 3: yours will differ. Check that each one could only be asked by
somebody who had thought about the job.
4. Is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?
5. It reads as a lack of interest, even when it is meant politely.
6. Pay and holiday. Hours also count.
4 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Self-motivated, results-driven: what those phrases prove
grammar.explanation:
Unit 2 taught you to build an adjective from two words with a hyphen.
A CV is full of them, and they divide sharply into two kinds: the ones that
describe work, which are useful, and the ones that describe you, which are
not. Knowing which is which is worth more than the list.
grammar.rule:
THE SELF-DESCRIBING SET — everybody writes these, and they prove nothing:
self-motivated, hard-working, detail-oriented, results-driven,
well-organised, team-focused
Every candidate claims them. None can be checked.

THE WORK-DESCRIBING SET — these carry information:
a three-year secondment      a cross-site rollout
a fixed-term contract        a client-facing role
a fully qualified electrician

THE TEST: could anybody claim the opposite about themselves?
Nobody writes I am poorly organised, so well-organised says nothing.
Not everybody can write a three-year secondment, so that one does.

WHAT TO WRITE INSTEAD: what you did.
Weak:   A results-driven, highly motivated technician.
Better: A technician who streamlined the checking and cut downtime by a fifth.
Only the second can be asked about.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Improve this profile line: A self-motivated, detail-oriented analyst.
1. Apply the test. Would anybody claim the opposite? No.
2. So both adjectives are unusable. Take them out.
3. Replace them with something you did, and a number.
Answer: An analyst who found a recurring fault in the returns data and cut
duplicate entries by a third.
Same person. The second version can be asked about; the first cannot.
grammar.mistake:
The self-describing adjectives feel like the safe choice, and they are the
expensive one: they use the top of the page, which is the part that gets read.
If you cannot imagine an interviewer asking a follow-up question about a
phrase, it should not be at the top of your CV.
grammar.tip: Could somebody claim the opposite? If not, the adjective is doing no work.
grammar.practice:
Mark each one USEFUL or EMPTY, and say why.
1. self-motivated   2. a three-year secondment   3. detail-oriented
4. a client-facing role   5. results-driven   6. a fully qualified electrician
7. well-organised   8. a cross-site rollout
Now rewrite these two as something an interviewer could ask about.
9. A self-motivated, detail-oriented analyst.
10. A hard-working and well-organised technician.
grammar.answers:
EMPTY: 1, 3, 5, 7. Nobody would claim the opposite of any of them.
USEFUL: 2, 4, 6, 8. Each is a fact somebody could check or ask about.
9. An analyst who found a recurring fault in the returns data and cut
   duplicate entries by a third.
10. A technician who oversaw two teams and sustained a 99 per cent uptime
    figure for eight months.
8 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Twice as many, by far the most: how big was the gap?
grammar.explanation:
Unit 2 put a degree word in front of a comparison: much cheaper, far better.
That says the gap is big. It does not say how big.
These structures do, and a CV or a report needs them, because a number is
what an interviewer remembers.
grammar.rule:
A MULTIPLE — twice, three times, half:
twice as many enquiries as last year
three times the volume of the second site
half the downtime we had before
The frame is: twice AS many AS, or twice THE number OF.

A PERCENTAGE OR AMOUNT:
twelve per cent above target
a fifth lower than the previous year
up by eleven, from thirty-four to forty-five

THE SUPERLATIVE, strengthened:
by far the most reliable of the three
easily the quickest route
one of the most experienced technicians on site
Note that one of the most takes a PLURAL noun after it: technicians.

AND THE COMPARISON THAT MOVES TOGETHER:
The more often it is checked, the fewer faults are found.

A warning. Every one of these invites the question compared with what?
Twice as many as WHAT. If you cannot answer that, do not write it.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You had 34 enquiries last year and 68 this year. Write it three ways.
1. As a multiple: twice as many enquiries as last year.
2. As an amount: up by thirty-four, from thirty-four to sixty-eight.
3. As a percentage: a hundred per cent up on last year.
Answer: all three are true. The first is the one people remember, and the
second is the one that survives a follow-up question.
grammar.mistake:
one of the most takes a plural, and learners write a singular.
No: one of the most experienced technician on site.
Yes: one of the most experienced technicians on site.
You are picking one out of a group, so the group has to be plural.
grammar.tip: Every comparison invites compared with what. Answer it in the same sentence.
grammar.practice:
Write each comparison.
1. 68 enquiries this year, 34 last year. (as a multiple)
2. The same figures, as an amount.
3. Target was 100, you reached 112. (as a percentage above)
4. Downtime halved. (using half)
5. It is the most reliable of three, clearly. (strengthen it)
6. She is among the most experienced on site. (use one of the most)
Now correct these.
7. one of the most experienced technician on site
8. We had twice as many enquiries.
grammar.answers:
1. twice as many enquiries as last year
2. up by thirty-four, from thirty-four to sixty-eight
3. twelve per cent above target
4. half the downtime we had before
5. by far the most reliable of the three
6. one of the most experienced technicians on site
7. technicianS — one of the most always takes a plural.
8. Twice as many as WHAT? Add the comparison: as last year.
6 or more right: good.

readings.title: The Top Third of the Page
readings.setting: Told by somebody who reads applications
readings.passage:
I read about four hundred applications a year and I have stopped pretending I read them all properly.
What I read properly is the top third of the first page. Everything below it gets skimmed.
That means the profile is the most valuable space on the document, and most people fill it with nothing.
Self-motivated. Hard-working. Detail-oriented. Results-driven.
There is a test I apply without meaning to. Would anybody write the opposite?
Nobody has ever sent me a CV saying they are poorly organised and easily distracted.
So those words carry no information, and they are sitting in the space that decides whether I keep reading.
What works is very simple and almost nobody does it.
Say what you did, and put a number on it.
A technician who streamlined the checking and cut downtime by a fifth is a person I can ask a question about.
The best profile I read last year was two lines long and had three numbers in it.
I could not tell you whether the candidate was self-motivated. I could tell you exactly what they had done, and I called them.

readings.title: The Preposition at the End
readings.setting: A page from a writing guide
readings.passage:
You may have been told never to end a sentence with a preposition.
That rule was invented in the seventeenth century by somebody who admired Latin, and it has never described English.
The company I worked for is correct, natural, and what every speaker says.
The company for which I worked is also correct, and it belongs to contracts and formal letters.
The difference is register, not rightness, and choosing the formal one in a conversation makes you sound stiff rather than careful.
There is one thing to know about the formal version.
Once the preposition moves to the front, who is no longer possible. It must be whom.
The person to whom it was sent, never the person to who it was sent.
And in the formal version nothing can be left out.
In the everyday one you can usually drop the relative word entirely: the company I worked for.
So the choice is between a short natural sentence and a longer formal one.
In an email, a CV or a conversation, use the first.
In a contract, or when quoting one, expect the second and be able to read it.

readings.title: Application: Maintenance Coordinator
readings.passage:
APPLICATION — MAINTENANCE COORDINATOR (Ref MC-208)

Profile
A technician with eleven years on site, four of them coordinating across two locations.
Streamlined the checking process and cut downtime by a fifth. Retained all four
contractors through the 2023 changeover.

Experience
2019 to present — Maintenance technician, northern site.
  Oversaw two teams. Implemented the new logging system in March 2022.
  Sustained a 99 per cent uptime figure for eight months, twice as long as the previous best.
2021 — Six-month secondment to the southern site, from which the current system was adapted.
2016 to 2019 — Electrician, contract work.
  The firm I worked for closed in 2019.

Competencies addressed
Working to a deadline: August 2022 shutdown, two staff short, finished a day early.
Liaising across sites: negotiated a shared parts store with the southern manager.

Referees
Two named overleaf, both of whom have been asked.

Questions for the panel
What would you want done in the first three months?
Is there anything in this application you would like me to expand on?

comprehension.q: Which part of an application does the writer read properly?
comprehension.a: The top third of the first page.
comprehension.why: Stated in the second line; everything below it gets skimmed.

comprehension.q: What test does the writer apply, without meaning to?
comprehension.why: Nobody claims to be poorly organised, so well-organised carries no information.

comprehension.q: Why are the empty adjectives worse than merely useless?
comprehension.a: They occupy the space that decides whether the reader keeps reading.
comprehension.why: The writer calls the profile the most valuable space on the document.

comprehension.q: What did the best profile the writer read last year contain?
comprehension.why: Stated at the end, and the writer called that candidate.

comprehension.q: Where did the rule against ending with a preposition come from?
comprehension.a: The seventeenth century, from somebody who admired Latin.
comprehension.why: The article says it has never described English.

comprehension.q: What is the real difference between the two versions?
comprehension.why: Both are correct; one belongs to speech and one to contracts.

comprehension.q: What happens to 'who' when the preposition moves to the front?
comprehension.why: To who is not possible once the preposition precedes it.

comprehension.q: How long was the applicant's uptime figure sustained, and how does the application make that meaningful?
comprehension.a: Eight months, described as twice as long as the previous best.
comprehension.why: The comparison answers the question 'compared with what'.

comprehension.q: What two competency examples does the applicant give, and what makes each one an answer?
comprehension.a: The August shutdown and the shared parts store. Each names a situation, an action and a result.
comprehension.why: Both are cases rather than claims, which is what a competency question asks for.

comprehension.q: Find the formal relative clause and the everyday one in this application.
comprehension.a: 'both of whom have been asked' and 'from which the current system was adapted' are formal; 'The firm I worked for closed in 2019' is everyday.
comprehension.why: The formal ones put the preposition in front; the everyday one leaves it at the end.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Say it twice
speaking.instructions:
Say each one twice: the everyday way, then the formal way.
1. I worked for a company. It closed in 2019.
2. I sent it to a person. They never replied.
3. We moved from a site. It is now a car park.
4. She reported to a manager. He has since left.
Models:
The company I worked for closed in 2019.
The company for which I worked closed in 2019.
Tap the mic. Say all four pairs. Tap again and listen.
Check: in the formal version, did who become whom?
Which of the two would you use on the telephone?
speaking.tutor: Say your four pairs and ask the tutor which version belongs in an email.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Where the stress falls in a job name
speaking.instructions:
Job names built with -ician, -ist and -ant put the stress in predictable places.
Listen and repeat. The capitals show the stress.
tech-NI-cian      e-lec-TRI-cian      mu-SI-cian
AN-a-lyst         SPE-cial-ist        SCI-en-tist
con-SUL-tant      prac-TI-tion-er
-ician always puts the stress on the part just before the ending.
-ist keeps the stress where the root word had it.
Now say these three lines.
Two technicians and an electrician cover the whole site.
The analyst and the consultant disagreed about the figures.
We need a specialist in the older machines.
Tap the mic. Say the lines. Tap again and listen.
Check: in technician and electrician, is the stress on the NI and the TRI?
speaking.tutor: Say the eight job names and ask the tutor which one you stressed wrongly.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Four sentences, one example
speaking.instructions:
Answer this out loud: tell me about a time when you had to work to a deadline.
Use exactly four sentences, in this order.
1. The situation.
2. What you were asked to do.
3. What you did.
4. The result, with a number in it.
A model:
We were two staff short over the August shutdown.
I was asked to cover the checking.
I streamlined the order of the checks and liaised with the yard directly.
We finished a day early and the backlog cleared by the third.
Invent whatever you like. Tap the mic and say your four sentences.
Tap again and listen.
Check: is there a number in sentence four?
Did sentence three say what YOU did, not what the team did?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your four sentences and ask which one an interviewer would follow up.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: the top third of the page
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
I read about four hundred applications a year and I have stopped pretending I read them all properly.
What I read properly is the top third of the first page.
That means the profile is the most valuable space on the document, and most people fill it with nothing.
Self-motivated. Hard-working. Detail-oriented.
There is a test I apply without meaning to. Would anybody write the opposite?
Nobody has ever sent me a CV saying they are poorly organised.
What works is very simple. Say what you did, and put a number on it.
The best profile I read last year was two lines long and had three numbers in it.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. How many applications does the speaker read a year?
2. Which part do they read properly?
3. What test do they apply?
4. What was the best profile like?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 about four hundred. 2 the top third of the first page.
3 would anybody write the opposite. 4 two lines, with three numbers in it.
speaking.tutor: Summarise the advice in two sentences and ask the tutor what you would change on your own CV.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Three questions for the panel
speaking.instructions:
You are at the end of an interview and they ask whether you have any questions.
Say three aloud: one about the work, one about the problem they are solving,
and one about what happens next.
Models:
What does a typical week look like in this post?
What made the post become available?
Is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?
Now say three of your own, for a job you invent.
Tap the mic. Ask your three questions. Tap again and listen.
Check: could any of your questions have been asked by somebody who had not
read the advertisement? If so, replace it.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor your three questions and ask which one it would most want to answer.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: talk me through it
speaking.instructions:
Talk through your working history for two minutes, real or invented.
Cover these four, in this order:
where you started and what you did there
one thing you coordinated, oversaw, streamlined or implemented
one result, with a number and a comparison
what you would want to do next, and why this post
Use at least three verbs from group 3 and at least one comparison with a size on it.
Do not use a single self-describing adjective.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: did any hard-working or self-motivated get in?
Does every comparison answer the question compared with what?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your two minutes and ask whether any claim could not be checked.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Eight relative clauses, two ways
writing.prompt:
Join each pair twice: once the everyday way, with the preposition at the end,
and once the formal way, with it in front.
a) I worked for a company. It closed in 2019.
b) I sent it to a person. They never replied.
c) We moved from a site. It is now a car park.
d) She reported to a manager. He has since left.
Then rewrite these two using where or when.
e) the site at which we worked
f) the day on which it happened
writing.model:
a) The company I worked for closed in 2019.
   The company for which I worked closed in 2019.
b) The person I sent it to never replied.
   The person to whom I sent it never replied.
c) The site we moved from is now a car park.
   The site from which we moved is now a car park.
d) The manager she reported to has since left.
   The manager to whom she reported has since left.
e) the site where we worked
f) the day when it happened
writing.starter: a) The company I worked for …
writing.criteria:
Every formal version uses whom or which, never who.
Every everyday version leaves the preposition at the end.
At least two everyday versions drop the relative word entirely.
e and f correctly converted to where and when.
writing.support: Write the everyday version first. Then move the preposition to the front and fix what follows it.
writing.extension: Write one sentence where the formal version would be right, and say what document it belongs to.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Three competency answers
writing.prompt:
Write four-sentence answers to three competency questions.
Situation, task, action, result. A number in every result.
a) Tell me about a time when you had to work to a deadline.
b) Give me an example of a problem you solved.
c) Describe a situation where you disagreed with a decision.
Invent everything. Use a different verb from group 3 in each action sentence.
writing.model:
a) We were two staff short over the August shutdown.
   I was asked to cover the checking.
   I streamlined the order of the checks and liaised with the yard directly.
   We finished a day early and the backlog cleared by the third.
b) Duplicate entries were appearing in the returns data every month.
   I was asked to find out why.
   I coordinated a check across both sites and traced it to one form.
   Duplicates fell by a third within two months.
c) The new logging system was going to be rolled out in one week.
   I was asked to prepare the northern site.
   I negotiated a two-week rollout instead and implemented it in stages.
   We lost four hours of downtime rather than the twenty forecast.
writing.criteria:
Each answer has exactly four sentences, in the right order.
Each result contains a number.
Each action sentence uses a different verb from group 3, and says what YOU did.
No self-describing adjectives anywhere.
writing.support: Write the four results first, with their numbers. Build each answer backwards from its result.
writing.extension: Write the follow-up question an interviewer would ask about one of your answers, and answer it.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Rewrite a profile
writing.prompt:
Here are three profiles full of empty adjectives.
Rewrite each one so that every claim could be asked about, and put a number in each.
a) A self-motivated, detail-oriented analyst with excellent communication skills.
b) A hard-working and well-organised technician who is passionate about quality.
c) A results-driven team player seeking a challenging new opportunity.
Then write one sentence saying what test you applied.
writing.model:
a) An analyst who found a recurring fault in the returns data and cut duplicate
   entries by a third in two months.
b) A technician who oversaw two teams and sustained a 99 per cent uptime figure
   for eight months, twice as long as the previous best.
c) A coordinator who retained all four contractors through a full changeover and
   negotiated a shared parts store across two sites.

The test was whether anybody would write the opposite about themselves.
writing.length: Three rewrites plus one sentence, about 90 to 120 words.
writing.criteria:
No self-describing adjective survives in any of the three.
Every rewrite contains at least one number.
Every rewrite uses a verb from group 3 or group 4.
The closing sentence states the test, not a preference.
writing.support: Underline every adjective in the original and ask whether anybody would claim its opposite.
writing.extension: Write your own real profile in two lines with three numbers in it.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A complete application
writing.prompt:
Write an application for a post you invent, in the style of Reading 3:
Profile, Experience, Competencies addressed, Referees, Questions for the panel.
The Profile must contain at least two numbers and no empty adjectives.
Experience must contain one formal relative clause and one everyday one.
Competencies must give two cases, each with a result.
Questions must include one about the work and one about what happens next.
writing.model:
Profile. A technician with eleven years on site, four of them coordinating across
two locations. Streamlined the checking and cut downtime by a fifth.
Experience. 2019 to present, northern site. Oversaw two teams and implemented the
new logging system in March 2022. Sustained 99 per cent uptime for eight months,
twice as long as the previous best. 2021, a six-month secondment to the southern
site, from which the current system was adapted. The firm I worked for before that
closed in 2019.
Competencies. Working to a deadline: August 2022, two staff short, finished a day early.
Liaising across sites: negotiated a shared parts store with the southern manager.
Referees. Two named overleaf, both of whom have been asked.
Questions. What would you want done in the first three months?
Is there anything in this application you would like me to expand on?
writing.length: A full application, about 160 to 210 words.
writing.criteria:
The Profile has two or more numbers and no empty adjectives.
One formal relative clause and one everyday one, both correct.
Two competency cases, each with a situation, an action and a numbered result.
Two questions, one of which invites the panel to raise a doubt.
writing.support: Write the Competencies section first. The Profile is a summary of it, so it is easier second.
writing.extension: Write the one line in your application a panel would challenge, and the answer you would give.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Everyday, or formal?
activities.instructions:
Write each one both ways.
1. I worked for a company. It closed in 2019.
2. I sent it to a person. They never replied.
3. We moved from a site. It is now a car park.
4. She reported to a manager. He has since left.
5. I applied for a post. It was withdrawn.
Now rewrite using where or when.
6. the site at which we worked
7. the day on which it happened
Now correct these.
8. the person to who it was sent
9. the company which I worked for it
activities.answers:
1. The company I worked for closed. / The company for which I worked closed.
2. The person I sent it to never replied. / The person to whom I sent it never replied.
3. The site we moved from is now a car park. / The site from which we moved is now a car park.
4. The manager she reported to has since left. / The manager to whom she reported has since left.
5. The post I applied for was withdrawn. / The post for which I applied was withdrawn.
6. the site where we worked  7. the day when it happened
8. to whom  9. the company I worked for (the it was doubled)
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Say the everyday version aloud first. If it sounds natural, it is right.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Build the four parts
activities.instructions:
For each question, write four lines: situation, task, action, result.
1. Tell me about a time when you had to work to a deadline.
2. Give me an example of a problem you solved.
3. Describe a situation where you disagreed with a decision.
Now answer these.
4. Which of these is a scenario question, not a competency one?
   a) What would you do if a delivery arrived late?
   b) Tell me about a time when a delivery arrived late.
5. Rewrite as a case: 'I work well under pressure and I am very organised.'
activities.answers:
1 to 3: yours will differ. Check each against four things.
The situation is one sentence. The task says what YOU were asked to do.
The action uses a verb like coordinated, streamlined, negotiated or liaised.
The result contains a number.
4. (a) is the scenario question. It has not happened, so it takes a second
   conditional. (b) is the competency question and takes a real case.
5. Any four-part example. If yours has no number, add one.
4 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the result first, with its number. Then work backwards to the situation.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Questions worth asking
activities.instructions:
Write questions for a job you invent.
1. One about the work itself.
2. One about the problem they are trying to solve.
3. One about what happens next.
4. One that invites them to raise a doubt about you.
Now answer these.
5. Why is 'no, you have covered everything' a poor answer?
6. Name two things that belong to the offer rather than the interview.
7. How many questions should you have ready, and how many should you ask?
activities.answers:
1 to 4: yours will differ. Test each one: could somebody who had not read the
advertisement have asked it? If yes, replace it.
4 should be close to: is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?
5. It reads as a lack of interest, even when it is meant politely.
6. Pay and holiday. Hours also count.
7. Have three ready, ask two, keep the third in case one is answered.
5 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write each question, then write the answer you would expect. If you can predict it, the question is weak.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Useful, or empty?
activities.instructions:
Mark each USEFUL or EMPTY, and say why in three words.
1. self-motivated  2. a three-year secondment  3. detail-oriented
4. a client-facing role  5. results-driven  6. a fully qualified electrician
7. well-organised  8. a cross-site rollout  9. passionate about quality
10. a fixed-term contract
Now rewrite these two.
11. A self-motivated, detail-oriented analyst.
12. A hard-working and well-organised technician.
activities.answers:
EMPTY: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Nobody would claim the opposite of any of them.
USEFUL: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Each is a checkable fact.
11. An analyst who found a recurring fault in the returns data and cut
    duplicate entries by a third.
12. A technician who oversaw two teams and sustained 99 per cent uptime for
    eight months.
10 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, try to write the opposite as a CV claim. If you cannot, the phrase is empty.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Put a size on it
activities.instructions:
Write each comparison.
1. 68 enquiries this year, 34 last year. (as a multiple)
2. The same figures, as an amount.
3. Target was 100, you reached 112. (as a percentage above)
4. Downtime halved. (using half)
5. It is the most reliable of three, clearly. (strengthen it)
6. She is among the most experienced on site. (use one of the most)
7. The more it is checked, the fewer faults appear. (write the frame)
Now correct these.
8. one of the most experienced technician on site
9. We had twice as many enquiries.
activities.answers:
1. twice as many enquiries as last year
2. up by thirty-four, from thirty-four to sixty-eight
3. twelve per cent above target
4. half the downtime we had before
5. by far the most reliable of the three
6. one of the most experienced technicians on site
7. The more often it is checked, the fewer faults are found.
8. technicianS  9. twice as many as WHAT? Add the comparison.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: After each one, ask compared with what. If the sentence does not say, it is not finished.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Name what you did
activities.instructions:
Each line is vague about what the person actually did. Rewrite it with a verb
from group 3 and a result from group 4, and put a number in.
1. I was involved in the move to the new system.
2. I helped with the contractors.
3. I worked on the checking process.
4. I was part of the team that dealt with the shutdown.
5. I had responsibility for two sites.
activities.answers:
Yours will differ. Each should name what YOU did and what changed.
1. I implemented the new logging system across both sites in March 2022.
2. I negotiated the contracts and retained all four contractors.
3. I streamlined the checking process and cut downtime by a fifth.
4. I coordinated the August shutdown two staff short and finished a day early.
5. I oversaw two sites and sustained 99 per cent uptime for eight months.
Note what disappears: involved in, helped with, worked on, part of.
All four hide whether you did it or watched it.
4 or 5 right: good.
activities.solo: Circle every vague verb first: involved, helped, worked on, part of. Replace each one.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the application
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. How many years has the applicant been on site, and how many coordinating?
2. What was implemented, and when?
3. How is the uptime figure made meaningful?
4. Copy the formal relative clause and the everyday one.
5. Copy the two competency cases and say what each result is.
6. Which of the two questions to the panel invites them to raise a doubt?
activities.answers:
1. Eleven years on site, four of them coordinating.
2. The new logging system, in March 2022.
3. It is compared: twice as long as the previous best.
4. Formal: 'from which the current system was adapted' and 'both of whom have
   been asked'. Everyday: 'The firm I worked for closed in 2019.'
5. The August shutdown — finished a day early. The parts store — negotiated
   a shared store across two sites.
6. 'Is there anything in this application you would like me to expand on?'
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the application with a pen and circle every number before you answer.

quizzes.q: The person ___ it was sent never replied. (formal, with the preposition in front)
quizzes.why: Once a preposition moves in front, who is impossible and whom is compulsory. The everyday version avoids it: the person I sent it to.

quizzes.q: The company ___ I worked closed in 2019. (the formal version)
quizzes.why: In the formal version the preposition moves in front and takes which after it. The everyday version puts it at the end: the company I worked for.

quizzes.q: 'Tell me about a time when you worked to a deadline.' What is it asking for?
options: What you would do in future.
quizzes.why: It is a competency question, and it is answered with a case: situation, task, action, result. Everybody says yes to the opinion version.

quizzes.q: Which part of a four-part competency answer is most often left out?
quizzes.why: The result is what the interviewer remembers, and a number is what makes it a result rather than a claim.

quizzes.q: At the end of an interview you are asked whether you have questions. Which is the best?
options: Is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?
quizzes.a: Is there anything in my application you would like me to expand on?
quizzes.why: It lets you repair a doubt before it becomes a decision. Holiday belongs to the offer, and the first reads as a lack of interest.

quizzes.q: Which CV phrase carries actual information?
quizzes.why: Apply the test: would anybody claim the opposite? Nobody writes that they are poorly motivated, so the other three say nothing.

quizzes.q: Why are empty adjectives worse than merely useless on a CV?
options: They occupy the space that decides whether you are read.
quizzes.a: They occupy the space that decides whether you are read.
quizzes.why: The profile is the top third of the first page, which is the part that gets read properly. Spending it on unverifiable claims is the cost.

quizzes.q: 68 this year against 34 last year: ___ as many enquiries as last year.
quizzes.why: The frame is twice AS many AS. Double and twofold do not take as, and two times is American rather than British usage.

options: one of the most experienced technicians
one of the most experienced technician
one of the more experienced technician
quizzes.a: one of the most experienced technicians
quizzes.why: one of the most picks one out of a group, so the noun has to be plural.

quizzes.q: 'We had twice as many enquiries.' What is missing?
quizzes.why: Every comparison invites the question compared with what. If the sentence cannot answer it, the claim is not finished.

quizzes.q: Which sentence names what the person actually did?
options: I was involved in the move to the new system.
I implemented the new logging system across both sites.
I was part of the team that dealt with the shutdown.
quizzes.a: I implemented the new logging system across both sites.
quizzes.why: Involved in, helped with and part of all hide whether you did it or watched it. implement names the action.

quizzes.q: 'What would you do if a delivery arrived late?' How is this answered?
options: With a real example from the past.
With a list of your strengths.
quizzes.why: It is a scenario question: it has not happened. A competency question begins 'tell me about a time when' and takes a real case instead.

teacherNotes.note: The plan's patterns here were profession suffixes, the register of a CV, and answering with evidence. Only the third matches a code. The codes placed are 8Ug.01 (questions that develop ideas), 8Ug.14 (compound and participle adjectives, and comparative structures for degree) and 8Us.03 (relative clauses including with prepositions). The profession suffixes survive in group 1 and in Speaking 2, where they are a pronunciation point rather than a pattern.

Relative clauses with prepositions are taught nowhere below this unit, despite four earlier cards on relative clauses. It is the code's own example (from where, to whom) and the reason this unit holds 8Us.03.

whom is widely believed to be optional. After a preposition it is not, and that is the only position where the rule is still live. Teach it there and nowhere else: 'the person whom I saw' is unnecessary; 'the person to whom I wrote' is required.

Learners answer competency questions with claims because their first language interview culture may genuinely want claims. Card 2's four-part shape is the fix, and Practice 2 asks for it in note form first so the shape is learned before the wording.
'one of the most experienced technician' is very persistent. The noun is plural because you are selecting from a group; say that rather than stating the rule.

Card 4 asks learners to delete phrases many of them have been taught to use, sometimes by employment advisers. The card does not say those advisers were wrong; it gives the test and lets the learner apply it. Reading 1 is written from the reader's side for the same reason — it is evidence, not an instruction.

Writing 4 is the unit's real assessment: a complete application in which all five cards have to work at once. Its support line tells learners to write the competencies first, because the profile is a summary of them and is far easier written second.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say the company I worked for, and the company for which I worked.
I know that whom is required once the preposition moves in front.
I can answer an interview question with a situation, a task, an action and a result.
I put a number in the result.
I can tell a competency question from a scenario question.
I have three questions ready for the end of an interview.
I can tell an empty CV adjective from one that carries information.
I answer the question compared with what, in the same sentence.

assignment.title: The application, and the interview that follows it
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write a complete application for a post you invent, in about 200 words:
Profile, Experience, Competencies addressed, Referees, Questions for the panel.
The Profile must contain at least two numbers and no adjective anybody could claim.
Experience must contain one formal relative clause and one everyday one.
Use at least four verbs from group 3 and at least two comparisons with a size on them.
Part two. Write full four-part answers to two competency questions the panel would
ask you, based on what your application claims. Each must end with a number.
Part three. Write the three questions you would have ready for the end, and say
which two you would ask and why.
Part four. Take your own Profile, rewrite it badly using four empty adjectives,
and write one sentence on what a reader loses.
assignment.submissionType: An application, two interview answers and a short analysis
